item.title: Jingisukan Guide: Hokkaido's Grilled Lamb BBQ & Where to Eat
item.description: Jingisukan (“Genghis Khan”) is Hokkaido’s beloved grilled-mutton barbecue, a smoky, sociable feast named for the dome-shaped grill said to resemble a warrior’s helmet. Diners cook lamb or mutton and a pile of vegetables — onions, beansprouts, cabbage, pumpkin — over the convex iron grill, where juices run down to flavour the veg around the rim. Washed down with ice-cold beer in a summer beer garden or a lively grill house, it’s one of Hokkaido’s most fun and convivial meals.

item.title: Sapporo Beer Garden Guide: Museum, Beer Hall & Summer
item.description: Sapporo is the birthplace of Japanese beer, and the Sapporo Beer Garden is the place to toast it. Set in a handsome red-brick complex that once brewed the nation’s beer, the site pairs the only Beer Museum in Japan with grand beer halls where the classic Hokkaido feast — all-you-can-eat jingisukan (grilled lamb) with all-you-can-drink beer — has been served for generations. In summer, the city throws an even bigger party: a vast open-air beer garden takes over Odori Park.

item.title: Hokkaido Food Guide: Crab, Uni, Soup Curry, Ramen & Dairy
item.description: Hokkaido’s food culture has an unusual characteristic for Japan: it is genuinely young. The island’s large-scale settlement began in the 1870s, which means its food traditions are 150 years old — not the centuries-old layered cuisine of Kyoto or the Edo period’s Tokyo. This created a food culture that is simultaneously Japanese and something else: lamb barbecue borrowed from sheep-farming experiments, soup curry developed in a pharmacy consultation, ramen styles refined from scratch in the post-war decades, and dairy that exists because American agricultural advisors arrived in 1870 and told Hokkaido to become the dairy region of Japan.
